budget.note: Section 5.2: frozen at the start, measured from the small tests that already exist, never guessed from an imagined platform. RTL is slow, so a single run registry serves several checks.

checker_note: `checkers` names the tools/r36 checker(s) that answer each package, as they were actually written. The planning version of this file guessed one name per package and two of the guesses were wrong: R36-04 is answered by rtl_tests.py rather than by the exporter, and R36-08's three cases are three separate checkers because a conformance suite, a mutation harness and a full inherited regression have nothing to share. The verifier keys on CASE ids rather than on these names, so a rename cannot make a package look complete.

claim_levels.engineering-ready: the shared package and interfaces exist and are tested; the specific platform is NOT verified
claim_levels.integration-tested: a reference adapter other than the built-in binding, closed through real RTL or a protocol loop to it. NOT a claim that a board ran anything.
claim_levels.note: Section 3.2. These are not interchangeable and each has to be recorded as itself.
claim_levels.operational: the existing simulated execution, with its tested range stated
claim_levels.platform-verified: reserved. Nothing in this stage may claim it.

fidelity.note: Section 5.2: on the same hardware implementation, pure engineering refactoring may not change the machine code or the device cycles of R3.5's frozen workloads. A necessary semantic change is identified separately and gets its own regression and performance evidence; it is not folded into a directory move called 'no behaviour change'.

A.may_then_claim: the engineering boundary and the compatibility rules are frozen

B.may_then_claim: the shared hardware and host interfaces are verified through a reference adapter

C.may_then_claim: the mainline can be handed to an independent platform branch

about: An audit of these checkers against section 6, clause by clause,
found a number of standards where the first demand was exercised and
a later one was not. Most were closed. These four were not, and are
recorded here rather than left to be rediscovered.
Each says what is not checked, why, and what would close it. None of
them is a claim that the thing is true; they are claims about what

items.not_checked: `proc; check -assert` -- the pass that reports latches and combinational loops -- runs over the exported shell module only. The whole exported hierarchy gets `hierarchy -check; check -noinit`, which cannot report either.
items.why: proc over the generated XLS units runs for upward of a quarter of an hour, and R3 v2's accepted r3v2-syn-tests already covers the core's internals on the same sources. Repeating it would buy a longer gate and no new fact.
items.would_close_it: running proc over the full exported hierarchy in a separate, slower job, or a yosys pass that reports latches without full proc.

items.not_checked: evidence is matched at the granularity of the 30 case IDs. A case that emits `passed: true` while exercising one of its three sub-demands is indistinguishable from a complete one.
items.why: there is no machine-readable decomposition of section 6's clauses into sub-conditions, so there is nothing to match against. Writing one is a transcription of the contract and would itself need checking against the contract.
items.would_close_it: a per-sub-clause inventory in this file, with each checker tagging which sub-clause each log line answers. The audit that found this list is the manual version of it.

items.not_checked: an artifact needing a capability the session's hardware lacks is not loaded and refused; the case records in prose that such an artifact cannot be produced.
items.why: the compiler refuses to emit an instruction the target does not publish, so there is no way to build the artifact through the product path. Constructing one by editing a compiled artifact would test the loader against something the compiler cannot make.
items.would_close_it: a capability field in the artifact manifest that the loader checks independently of the instructions, and a hand-edited artifact that sets it. MUT-CAPABILITY covers the other direction -- a target claiming a capability the hardware lacks.

items.not_checked: reproducibility is established for the downstream rehearsal (R36-HAND-01 runs it twice and requires the same cycles and the same conformance verdicts) but not for the full simulated execution: the 26-suite regression and the fidelity measurement are each run once.
items.why: running the inherited regression twice doubles the longest part of the gate for a property the per-suite oracles already constrain. The stochastic workload is the only one that does not return the same number twice, and fidelity.py already reads it five times and compares medians against the measured spread.
items.would_close_it: a second full regression run compared suite by suite, in a job of its own.

mutation_note: `detector` is the checker that ACTUALLY catches each mutation, established by breaking the thing and seeing which checker fails. Where it differs from the planning guess the guess is kept as `detector_planned`, because the difference is information: M03's wrong epoch is caught by the conformance suite rather than by R36-IO-03, since the file mailbox has no epoch and the socket binding does; and M04's early completion is caught by the memory boundary's value checks rather than by R36-IO-02, because a completion reported too early shows up as wrong data, not as a protocol error. tools/r36/mutation_tests.py runs a CLEAN control of each distinct detector first, so a detector that fails for its own reasons cannot be credited with a catch.

mutations.what: return a reply under the wrong epoch
report completion before the writes are visible
drop a dependency from the export
forge a PASS or hide a missing case

note: doc/phase3_6_tasks_and_acceptance.md section 6. Ten packages, thirty standards. Section 8 is explicit about what the sign-off does NOT mean: not that an FPGA runs, not that an ASIC is implemented, not that the project is production-signed.
owner_note: R36-EV-02 asks for evidence AND an owner for every standard. These are roles rather than people -- doc/r36_handoff.md section 9 says the same -- and the point of naming one is that a change to a public interface has a place to be argued about, not that there is a committee. The verifier requires the field to be present and non-empty; it cannot check that somebody is actually doing the job.
